objectives: LO 4.1.1: Explain why bond prices move opposite to interest rates and price a bond from its cash flows
LO 4.1.2: Use duration and convexity to estimate how much a bond's price will change when rates move
LO 4.2.1: Compare fundamental and technical analysis and connect each to MPT and the EMH
LO 4.2.2: Judge how debt financing changes ROE, risk, dividend growth and stock value
LO 4.3.1: Value a stock with the no-growth, constant growth and multistage DDMs, FCFE and capitalized earnings
LO 4.3.2: Use P/E, PEG, P/FCF and P/S to decide whether a stock looks cheap or expensive
synthesis: Module 4 turns the risk ideas from earlier modules into prices. Duration quantifies the interest-rate risk in every bond allocation and drives horizon matching in client plans, while the DDMs plug a CAPM required return and a growth rate from financial-statement analysis into an intrinsic value. Relative ratios and financial-statement analysis are the everyday tools for deciding whether a recommendation is worth its price.

example.title: Is Kestrel worth $54 to Selma?
example.html:
Kestrel just paid a $2.40 dividend, expected to grow 4% a year. Selma requires 9%.

  1. D1 = 2.40 × 1.04 = $2.496
  2. V = 2.496 ÷ (0.09 − 0.04) = $49.92
  3. Price $54 > value $49.92 → overvalued for Selma; don't buy at $54.

Sensitivity: if her required return fell to 8%, V = 2.496 ÷ 0.04 = $62.40 — small changes in r − g swing the answer a lot.

keyNumbers: N = years × 2, PMT = coupon ÷ 2, I/YR = market yield, FV = par
V = D<sub>0</sub>(1 + g) ÷ (r − g); g must be < r
mustKnow: Duration falls as coupon or market yield rises and grows with maturity; a zero's duration equals its maturity
Match a bond's duration, not its maturity, to the client's time horizon
Positive convexity: duration understates gains and overstates losses; callable and mortgage-backed bonds show negative convexity
Premium bond: CY > YTM > YTC; discount bond: CY < YTM < YTC
Leverage raises ROE and EPS but adds fixed interest that hurts in a contraction; low ROA vs. ROE signals leverage
Constant growth fits mature firms; multistage fits growth-phase firms; FCFE fits non-dividend payers
Intrinsic value above price = undervalued; relative methods need a peer or industry benchmark
traps: Using the coupon rate as y in the duration formula
Plugging D<sub>0</sub> into the Gordon model without growing it to D<sub>1</sub>
Multiplying ROE by the payout ratio instead of the retention rate
Treating technical analysis as useful under any form of the EMH
Picking the lowest P/E without adjusting for growth (use PEG)
tips: Predict premium or discount before pricing a bond; it catches calculator entry errors
If a YTM is given in a duration question, use the (1 + y) version of the formula
In multistage problems, add the terminal value to the last high-growth year's cash flow before taking the NPV
